newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Dec 30.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Dec 30.

text.p: Four fishermen died and one was missing early this morning after a fishing boat and a container ship collided near the entrance to Wellington Harbour. They were believed to have been trapped in the upturned hull of the boat. One person from the 15-metre fishing boat was winched to safety soon after the collision. Police divers were still searching for the missing person early this morning. Page 1.

The leading yacht in the round-the-world yacht challenge, Group Four, with Lower Hutt man Grant Winfield on it, was sailing towards Wellington last night and was expected to arrive early today. The rest of the 14 yachts in the BT Global Challenge are expected over the next five days. In second place is Save the Children and third is Toshiba Wave Warrior. The race is promoted as the "the world's toughest yacht race" because the yachts are travelling the "wrong way" around the world, from east to west, against prevailing winds and currents. Page 1.

The Fisheries Ministry has begun formal consultations over how much of the bill for its services the industry should pick up, and has issued a White Paper on the new cost-recovery system. Ministry spokesperson Robert Brewer said the paper would be made public after the fishing industry had had a few days to study it. Page 2.

The MP for Manakau East, Labour's Ross Robertson, wants South Auckland classified as a special needs area because of the diverse range of cultures. Robertson said the area was falling behind other parts of the country in education, health, housing and employment. "What concerns me is that we have a very diverse ethnic background, which means that many of the people living in this area are not aware of their entitlement and the recourse that are available to them." Page 2.

Maori and Pacific Island achievement levels are improving but still lag behind those of the general population, Education Ministry briefing papers to the government say. "Maori students, as well as Pacific Island students, are disproportionately represented amongst the minority of students who leave the schooling system with no, or very low, qualifications," the ministry says. Page 3.

Overseas retail groups, mainly Australian, are keeping up the demand for prime quality retail space in New Zealand, according to real estate group Knight Frank. In its latest Retail Review, Knight Frank says an increasing number of international retailers are turning their attention to New Zealand and the property sector has to keep pace. Page 10.

Most people in business will be glad to see the back of 1996. For many, especially those in the export sector, it was a tough year made worse by political uncertainties. The trouble is that 1997 doesn't look much better, certainly in the short term. Statistics suggest the economy is at the bottom of a trough, and Reserve Bank governor Don Brash, in an unexpectedly cautious December monetary statement, made it clear he wants more of the same. Page 10.
The New Zealand economy is likely to accelerate in 1997, fuelled by increased government spending that could push interest rates up by the year's end, analysts say.

High tides could be the cause of much of the damage as Cyclone Fergus sweeps south today. In a phenomenon known as storm surge, onshore winds and falling air pressure will add as much as a metre to high tides from North Cape to Tauranga, with the wind and the waves on top of that. Although Fergus will have been downgraded from a tropical cyclone to an extra-tropical cyclone by the time it hits New Zealand, the chief meteorologist at the MetService, Augie Auer, said it was a "serious storm with great potential for serious impact on New Zealand". Page 1.

Interest rate increases by central bankers around the world will be the exception rather than the rule in 1997 even as growth picks up in many nations, according to surveys in 30 countries. This good news on borrowing costs is mostly related to the absence of rising prices for consumers and business, the nemesis of central bankers everywhere, analysts said.

Blue chip stocks rose modestly on Friday but closed at a record high, shrugging off weakness in technologies as portfolio managers snapped up large, relatively safe shares. The Dow Jones average closed 14.23 points higher at a record 6,560.91, topping the November 25 mark of 6,547.79. Friday's gains extended the Dow's rally to its eighth rise in a row.
